output.rationale: Teach the membrane model first, then require self-explanation and a repair cycle before a final recognition check.

essentialIdeas: Phospholipid bilayers are selectively permeable because hydrophobic tails block most polar or charged molecules while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily.
Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient without cellular energy, while active transport uses energy to move substances against the gradient.
completionEvidence: Explains why a phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable.
Distinguishes passive from active transport in a concrete example.
Produces an independent corrected explanation after feedback.

activities.label: Membrane model
activities.title: Membrane structure and movement
activities.body: Review the model and note the key relationship. Then move to the explanation prompt.

essentialIdeas: Phospholipid bilayers are selectively permeable because hydrophobic tails block most polar or charged molecules while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily.
Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient without cellular energy, while active transport uses energy to move substances against the gradient.

activities.label: Explain in your own words
activities.title: Why membranes are selective
activities.body: Explain the membrane model in your own words. Keep it to the two main ideas.
activities.concept: Why the bilayer is selectively permeable and how transport differs by energy use and gradient
activities.correctAnswer: The phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable because the hydrophobic interior blocks most polar or charged substances, while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily. Passive transport moves down a concentration gradient without energy, and active transport uses energy to move against the gradient.
activities.feedback: A complete answer names the hydrophobic barrier, the molecules it blocks or lets through more easily, and the energy difference between passive and active transport.

activities.label: Repair the explanation
activities.title: Fix the missing part
activities.body: Compare your answer with the model and correct any missing cause or energy detail.
activities.misconceptionSummary: The membrane works like a simple open fence, so any molecule can cross if it is small enough.
activities.concept: Correct the idea that small size alone controls crossing
activities.correctAnswer: Small size alone is not enough. The phospholipid bilayer has a hydrophobic interior that lets small nonpolar molecules cross more easily but blocks most polar or charged molecules unless transport proteins help.
activities.feedback: The repair should replace the open-fence idea with the hydrophobic barrier and the role of transport proteins.

activities.label: Explain again
activities.title: Say it again clearly
activities.body: Give a second explanation from memory. Use new wording, not the model's phrasing.
activities.concept: Independent explanation of membrane selectivity and transport energy
activities.correctAnswer: The phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable because its hydrophobic core makes it harder for most polar or charged molecules to cross, while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily. Passive transport does not use energy and goes down a gradient, while active transport uses energy to move against a gradient.
activities.feedback: This check looks for a fresh, accurate explanation that still includes the barrier, the gradient, and the energy difference.

activities.label: Transport recognition check
activities.title: Choose the transport type
activities.body: Pick the best answer for the example. One choice is correct.
activities.concept: Classify a transport example as passive or active
choices: A substance moves from high concentration to low concentration without energy.
A substance moves from low concentration to high concentration using energy.
A substance crosses only because the membrane is made of phospholipids.
A substance moves only when the cell releases water.
activities.correctAnswer: A substance moves from low concentration to high concentration using energy.
activities.feedback: Active transport requires energy and moves against the concentration gradient; passive transport moves down the gradient without energy.

activities.label: Wrap-up
activities.title: Quick reflection
activities.body: Name one part of today's model that changed or sharpened your thinking.

items.essentialIdea: Phospholipids form a hydrophobic core that blocks most polar or charged substances.

check.title: Phospholipid barrier
check.prompt: How does phospholipid structure make the membrane selectively permeable?
check.referenceAnswer: Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward, creating a core that resists most polar and charged molecules.
check.feedback: The key is the hydrophobic interior, not the outer heads.

items.essentialIdea: Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient without ATP; active transport uses ATP against it.

check.title: Compare transport types
check.prompt: How do passive transport and active transport differ in energy use and direction?
check.referenceAnswer: Passive transport moves down a concentration gradient without ATP, while active transport requires energy to move against a gradient.
check.feedback: The main contrast is both energy use and movement relative to the gradient.

recognitionCheck.title: Transport direction check
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which statement best describes active transport?
choices: It moves substances down their concentration gradient without ATP.
It moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP.
It moves only water across the membrane by diffusion.
It always uses channel proteins and no energy.
recognitionCheck.correctAnswer: It moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP.
recognitionCheck.feedback: Active transport requires energy and moves against the gradient.
